newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban step closer to mastery of Afghanistan.
newsitem.headline: Taleban step closer to mastery of Afghanistan.

text.p: The defeat of northern Afghan leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum has brought the Taleban movement a step closer to its goal of imposing a strict Islamic order throughout Afghanistan.
The Taleban, to Moscow's publicly voiced dismay, have brought Moslem militancy to the borders of fragile Central Asian states that once formed part of the old Soviet Union.

Pakistan, which has shown sympathy for the Taleban while denying charges that it actually spawned the movement, hastened to recognise the Taleban government in Kabul after last week's anti-Dostum revolt led to the fall of the north.
No other country has recognised the Taleban as the legitimate rulers of Afghanistan, whose seat at the United Nations and other international bodies remains contested.
Militarily, there seems little to stop the mainly ethnic Pashtun Taleban from crushing resistance by Karim Khalili's Shi'ite Moslem militia in the central town of Bamiyan.

The bearded Islamic warriors may be able to extend their sway over all but a northeastern pocket of Afghanistan held by renowned guerrilla chief Ahmad Shah Masood, an ethnic Tajik, if he chooses to hold out in his rugged Panjsher valley stronghold.
No one knows if the Taleban's dominance can bring lasting peace to this mountainous country, devastated by the Soviet occupation of the 1980s and factional fighting that followed.

The United Nations, whose envoys have had the thankless task of trying to mediate an end to the conflict, wants the formation of a broad-based government that would represent all of Afghanistan's ethnic, religious and political groups.
The Taleban are quite anxious to be seen as a pan-Afghan movement whose Islamic zeal sets it above ethnic politics.
Many Afghans, even those who do not share the Taleban's religious fervour, have been willing to submit to them if that is the price for the security and peace they crave.
Now the Taleban face the hard tasks of moulding fractious ethnic minorities into a single nation, rebuilding the broken economy and assuaging the fears of neighbouring countries.
General Abdul Malik's mutiny aaginst Dostum has, for the moment at least, ended opposition for the Taleban in the Uzbek-dominated parts of the northern plains.

But the Taleban's stated intention of imposing Islamic Sharia law in its full vigour, as in the rest of the country, may fuel resentment among fiercely independent Uzbeks accustomed to a much more free-wheeling version of Islam.
Malik himself, while endorsing plans to bring strict Sharia to the north, has also said he wants talks aimed at bringing Rabbani, Masood and Khalili into a broad-based government.
He may calculate that Uzbeks, Tajiks and Shi'ite Hazaras could then counter-balance the Pashtun power of the Taleban, and perhaps moderate some of their more radical impulses.
For the Taleban, reaching an accommodation with those they have scornfully dismissed as the tools of foreign powers might involve political compromises they have so far shunned.
Making deals with "criminals and traitors" such as Masood and Rabbani might confuse the Taleban's illiterate young troops, nurtured on dreams of martyrdom in the name of Islam.

Yet failure to pay more than lip service to Afghanistan's ethnic mosaic could stir up future trouble for the Taleban as they grapple with the challenge of governing the country and re-channelling the energies of the revolutionary armed movement.

The largely Sunni Moslem Taleban have already engendered deep suspicions in the mainly Shi'ite Iran. Accusations that the Taleban are a creation of Pakistan, the United States and Saudi Arabia surface frequently in the Iranian media.
Tajikistan, where Moslem guerrillas have been fighting a Russian-backed government in Dushanbe, fear the repercussions of the growing Taleban power on its delicate internal balance.
Uzbekistan and Turkemenistan are also nervous of Islamic fervour gaining ground among their mainly Moslem populations.

Yet Afghanistan also holds a key to regional prosperity as a possible route for pipelines to deliver gas from Turkmenistan to Pakistan and India, and oil from Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan and even Kazakhstan, to Pakistan and export markets beyond. The pipelines cannot be built until stability is restored in Afghanistan and international investors and lenders can deal with a government broadly accepted by the world community.
